answer is "blue cardboard". as for the first question, personally, when the climate negotiations began, i was more in favour of a taxation system. europe has lost on this issue. but what i know today is that if we lose in the carbon market, there will be no alternative instrument. the reason why the carbon market today does not provide incentives for transformation and carbon-neutral is that the price is too low and the incentive needs to be reinforced, in particular by obtaining auction revenues to finance the energy transition. it may not be the best system, but it is the only one that exists today, and that is why it needs to be improved. as for mr szymański's question, if you are professing today with mr mittal, and a number of big players, that the carbon market must be killed, it is that, in fact, you want to prevent the structure that allows innovation in the carbon market, that allows sobriety and that allows investment. by killing the carbon market, you also kill all the ulcos projects that were able to support the transformation and sustainability of the steel industry in europe.
mr president, there are those in this house who are defending the climate, and then there are the others. i don't accept that shortcut. today our commission, so liberal, is being interventionist. it's not the spirit of 2008 either. the price of carbon has fallen, partly because of the economic recession affecting our european industries, but also because of the efforts already made, since we are confident of meeting the emission reduction targets set for 2020. commissioner, you are interfering with a market system which was not designed for this. the postponement of quotas, which you are so keen to see artificially raised the price of co2, is only a short-term measure, which is detrimental to economic activity. but as you know, there is no reindustrialisation policy without an energy policy. on the one hand, there are the energy suppliers, who have an interest in seeing the cost of energy rise, and it is them that the commission is protecting. and then there are those who are the customers of these suppliers, our industries, our smes, who are already suffering so much. commissioner, you do not have the same energy to revive energy efficiency. is this the way to make europe love when one factory closes after another? i do not accept this technocratic europe, which is disconnected from the realities on the ground. i do not accept this europe which wants to increase energy prices arbitrarily in times of crisis. i do not accept a europe which undermines the confidence of external markets because it changes the rules of the game along the way. who will have the courage to tell our fellow citizens that europe wants to raise the price of energy? that's why i don't accept backloading.
member of the commission. − mr president, can i first say to ms sartori who, like a number of others, was concerned about the increase in electricity prices: i think it is very important here to put things in proportion. if you vote ‘yes’ to this, then the commission’s impact assessment, the big operators in this market, and those who on a daily basis analyse the implications of what we do – such as point carbon and bloomberg energy finance – all these specialists estimate that the maximum impact on the cost of co2 per tonne would be a return to the prices of last september, october and november. that is what we are talking about, and that is why i say let us put things into proportion. ms korhola and ms jordan and a number of others have said we should go for structural changes. ms jordan said we should devote our time to structural changes. i very much agree with this, but i just think that we have to see it like this: it is as if there is a patient who needs long-term matters to be tended to, but you firstly need to take care of more pressing matters. you need to do the first things first – and that is what backloading is trying to do. we will come back to these other things, but we need to do the first things first. mr szymański mentioned energy-intensive sectors, such as cement, steel and chemicals. i should just like to remind you all that they get most of their allowances for free. if they are very technologically advanced, they will indeed get all of their allowances for free. i should just like to remind you how they were identified: on the basis of a carbon price that was seven times what it is today. it is based on a eur 30 carbon price. mr ferreira mentioned that we should also have a regulatory approach. yes, of course. this is not the only instrument, but it is the key instrument. i happen to think that this is why it was no coincidence that this parliament, when adopting regulatory measures like the energy efficiency directive, asked the commission to look at short-term implications for emissions trading. this was because you wanted us to avoid contradictory policies. i thought that this was wise at that time. i still believe that it was a sensible thing that you asked for. i think that almost any economist would say that it would be a failure of the market if the cost of emitting co2 or the cost of polluting with co2 were as low as it is now. it was mr gierek who asked why they were doing this and who has been discussing it. well, we have been asked to do it by you yourselves – the european parliament. however, it was also discussed at an informal environmental council last year in april, so of course we also had the backing of member states to come forward and address this. to ms kolarska-bobińska who asked whether we could be sure that this would be done just once, i think that i have already addressed that matter in my first speech. of course, if this is part of the legislative measure we are taking, this is a guarantee. it could never be changed unless we came back to it. however, i have been very clear on this matter, including to the different groups. this is an extraordinary thing and not something that the commission takes lightly, so i see it very much as something we do once only, as i stated in my first comment. i would just like to say one thing: when you listen to this debate, you would think that we are already discussing the structural measures. however, i should like to remind you that all allowances stay in the system. it is not about removing allowances; that is for another discussion. this is only about when to auction allowances and in what quantities. however, we are trying to stop short-term overflowing in a market which is already overflowing and over-supplied. so that is basically what it is about. my final point: holger krahmer said that the rest of the world is not following us. well, that is not actually true when it comes to emissions trading. here, the rest of the world – korea, china and australia, to mention but a few – is actually starting to follow the european union’s example. i think it is quite interesting for this debate to note that, last week, china announced that it would come up with a proposal next month for a nationwide emissions trading scheme. would it not look just a bit foolish if europe did not get it right with its own emissions trading scheme when we have actually now managed to get some of our very big competitors to adopt or start adopting a market-based system? so this is also a test. the world is watching what we are doing; this is actually one of the areas where we are leading the world. mr president, my very last comment is that i understand that for those of you who think that we do not have a climate problem or who have always been against the market-based system, of course it makes sense to vote ‘no’ tomorrow. however, all of us who ultimately want this system, with its inherent challenges and the market-based principle guiding it, must be careful to get it right tomorrow. it is very interesting to discuss structural measures, but that takes time. europe needs innovation now. our competitors are moving, and they are moving fast. the call that we get from investors is this: please ensure that we get a stronger price signal for the shorter term, and then we would be ready to invest. i do not think europe can afford to reject this. i still very much hope that this parliament will deliver on a process that they themselves initiated in recent months.
in writing. the community's emissions trading scheme (ets) was intended to meet the objective of reducing greenhouse gas emissions, but the market is suffering from a surplus of allowances. by 2020, if nothing is done, the surplus could be 1.42 billion allowances. the price of carbon would then remain low and volatile, with no deterrent for industry. the european commission's backloading proposal, echoed in the matthias groote report, would reduce the quantity of quotas by 900 million by 2019. it is a good measure to clean up the carbon market, which has so far functioned in a biased way: as a system of subsidies for polluters. climate change is a global issue. the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has increased by 31% since 1750. the current rate of increase is unprecedented in 20,000 years. we have now entered a new geological era called the anthropocene. it is the tipping point when human activity becomes the determining factor in the evolution of the earth system. the time is critical and european leaders have clearly not yet fully grasped this.
in writing. i support the rejection of the european commission's proposal on carbon trading and its withdrawal because i oppose any intervention by the european commission in the current context. the commission is not satisfied with the low price of carbon because it has not foreseen the crisis and the slowdown in industrial activity. however, it is this same slowdown that is preventing us from intervening. we must not increase the pressure on european companies, because european jobs depend on it. changing the rules of a european system of polluting duties along the way is the best way to continue the relocation. the eu's most ambitious climate policy in the world must not take precedence over employment in europe. if the demand for polluting rights decreases in a period of economic downturn, it is not the responsibility of dg climate change to propose an intervention in the system in place. the commission could propose the creation of an independent european authority to regulate the carbon emissions system.
for the gue/ngl group mr president, this greenhouse gas emissions trading scheme is a very bad answer to a real problem. global warming is one of the major problems facing all of humanity. to solve it, therefore, requires drastically reducing greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in the areas of transport, but also in agriculture, heating, waste treatment and industrial production. this implies coordinated, decentralized, planned and strong actions linking industry, research, policy makers but also consumers. this would also mean the creation of a large european public service for energy and waste treatment, instead of sterile competition between the major national energy groups and between the different energy sources. the idea of solving the problem of greenhouse gas emissions by the market is dogmatic and vicious. dogmatic, because the market solves nothing. it is, on the contrary, the play of all speculation and all lobbying. the major international road hauliers are thus systematically favoured, while air transport is hampered. and yet, in 30 years, greenhouse gas emissions per passenger have been reduced by 50 percent. vicarious because this market of quotas will always allow the richest to continue to pollute with impunity while the poorest are rationed energy. the solution is not in a quota market, nor in the market at all, but in research and regulations which will involve everyone according to their responsibilities, including goods from countries which do not comply with any environmental rules.
on behalf of the s&d group. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the efforts made by european fishermen over many years to conserve mackerel can be described as exemplary. so much so that, as early as 2006, it was noted that mackerel stocks were returning to historically high levels. unfortunately, the fruits of these efforts have not benefited those who have consented to them. because as soon as the biomass of this species started to rise, we saw a real rush of icelandic and faroese fishermen on mackerel. the ecological consequences on biomass, as well as the reduction in european quotas, have not been long in coming and the economic situation of the union's fishermen is now in jeopardy. the whole european pelagic sector is concerned. in france, no less than 1 200 vessels are targeting or by-catching mackerel. probably as much in ireland and the uk. many of them were small-scale fishermen. reducing by-catch quotas will inevitably impact all their catches with an imminent landing obligation for discards which will make the situation extremely tense. if iceland and the faroe islands continue to ignore the state of biomass, the union fishermen will become the adjustment variable for the achievement of the mdg to which they alone will contribute. it is no longer a question of following the situation closely, madam commissioner, or simply communicating. it is urgent that the european institutions play their role as regulators and that these behaviours, which are irresponsible from an ecological and economic point of view, be punished. firstly, can we not consider including these states on the list of those that do not respect sustainable fishing? secondly, since we have special fishing agreements with these players, is there not a reason to question them in a global way?
madam president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i want to express my great disappointment in several respects on the issue of the distribution of mackerel quotas between coastal states. this conflict between the european union, iceland and the faroe islands undermines a long-standing agreement between states with common interests that enabled the sustainable management of resources. the unilateral and irresponsible increase in quotas by the faroe islands and iceland is leading to unsustainable exploitation of mackerel in the area. the unrealistic mackerel quotas required by iceland and the faroe islands are excessively high in comparison with their predecessors. as our colleague mr sánchez presedo has just said, the faroe islands have increased their quota fivefold between 2009 and 2012, and iceland has increased its quota from 2006 by 23 times. it's completely unreasonable and unjustified. we must safeguard the environmental, economic and commercial interests of all the actors involved. it is essential that negotiations resume. it is the sustainable development of our oceans that is at stake. within the european union, professionals accept strict rules and quotas. the european union is doing its utmost to preserve fisheries resources in these waters. but what is the union doing in the context of shared stocks with other countries? the 2012 regulation on unsustainable fisheries allows for the imposition of sanctions on states that do not cooperate in the management of a common stock and apply unsustainable management measures. the regulation provides for restrictions on imports of fish. what is the commission waiting for before adopting sanctions? this will certainly bring about a return to reason in iceland and the faroe islands. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the establishment of a european centre for the development of vocational training.
mr president, aerospace is one of the last industries where the union is still on a par with the united states and asia. this is the result of the historical involvement and investment of public authorities in member states such as germany, spain and france. without this intervention, the airbus a320, the cfm 56 jet or ariane would never have been born. without this intervention, tens of thousands of skilled jobs would have disappeared. today the member states, and particularly france, are sending very negative signals. eads believes that the withdrawal of france and spain will give 70% of the capital to private shareholders and remove almost all possibility of public intervention in strategic choices. by selling 3% of safran's shares, france loses the blocking minority over this group. the italian engine manufacturer avio, which is involved in the engine development of ariane, has just been sold to the american general electric. europe is selling off its aircraft industry to pay off its bank debt, even though the order books are full for ten years. it is urgent that our parliament solemnly calls on the member states and the commission to stop this selling of an industry vital to europe's future.

prime minister of finland. − mr president, as you have already mentioned, we received shocking news last night of what seems to be a bomb attack against civilians in boston. a number of people are dead and over a hundred injured. our thoughts are with the victims and with their families. we do not yet have a full picture of what happened and should wait to hear what the american authorities find out, but i will say this: no matter what proves to be the cause of these explosions, we europeans will stand by our american friends. i would like to thank you, mr president, for your invitation to address the european parliament today. this is a very special honour for me personally, because i have been active in european affairs all my adult life. thanks to european integration, i belong to a generation which has had more opportunities than the generations before. for example, i had the opportunity to complete part of my studies at the university of leicester in the uk. as an erasmus student i spent a year there studying european affairs. this experience opened my eyes to the importance of european integration. i had my erasmus year in a period of great optimism. finland had joined the european union. the implementation of the economic and monetary union was being accelerated. preparations for the next enlargement – which united europe – were gathering pace. mr president, today we live in more difficult and challenging times. we are in the middle of an important debate about europe’s future. i am therefore grateful for this opportunity to exchange views with parliament. i came here not only to speak, but also to listen. the debate on european integration is being overshadowed by the economic crisis. people worry about their jobs, their pensions, their children’s future. with far too many young people unemployed, it is easy to see why they are worried and even angry. the public mood in many parts of europe is pessimistic. let us be frank about it – personally, i fully understand this mood, but at the same time it worries me very deeply. we have all been forced to make very difficult choices during the financial crisis. consequently, nationalism and populism are on the move. these painful decisions have undermined people’s trust in the european project. my fear is that we will turn inward when we should open up, and that we will doubt each other’s motives when we should come together; that we will allow radical voices to lead the european debate when we should present a credible, pragmatic way forward. we should not let pressing economic and social challenges poison the whole idea of european integration, and we should not let the european debate be dominated by the far ends of the spectrum. some will blame the eu for all our troubles. others will say – often from outside europe – that we must create a fully-fledged united states of europe here and now, without raising the issue of democratic legitimacy. i also do not understand those who stir up divisions between the south and the north. divided we are weaker, because we lose our common-value base and our ability to build europe together. we simply cannot afford that. we have difficult decisions at hand but we must stay united. mr president, honourable members, it is our duty as political leaders to take the stage and present credible present solutions to europe’s political and economic challenges. we must explain to people why deeper pragmatic integration is the right way forward for europe. to regain people’s trust in the european project, we must make sure europeans find integration to be just and fair. this is no easy task. but we can go a long way if we work on european integration that benefits everyone. in other words, we need fair integration. i understand that people in different member states and in different personal situations may not find their life particularly fair right now. but can europe be more fair in the future? i think it can. to me, fair integration means that the european union continues to be founded on common values and rules that are truly respected by all and at all times. fair integration means that, while member states engage in ever-closer integration, they keep their own house in order. we should be able to rely on each other. but we cannot outsource all responsibility to the others. and most importantly, fair integration means that the european union functions in ways people can support and feel their own. it is a question of democratic legitimacy and accountability and ownership. you can see, ladies and gentlemen, that i am not talking about anything earth-shattering. all i am asking is that we take decisions on the basis of our common rules and then live by them, and that we seek common solutions where such are needed and do our homework so that each member state can trust the others. let me be clear: we need more europe and we need more national responsibility. we cannot have one without the other. mr. president, let me now explain how i see fair integration in practice. i will raise three issues and look at them from the point of view of fair integration. first, we must respect our common european values and the rules we have adopted together. the european union is so much more than a free trade area – it is a community of shared values. we must defend european values also when they are challenged from within. failing to do so will undermine the union’s credibility – not only in the eyes of the world, but also in the eyes of our own people and citizens. if we overlook corruption and breaches of the rule of law, or if we fail to curb tax evasion and tax havens, we undermine our own efforts to build a better europe. as a union of values, we have decided that integration is based on democracy. we have decided to replace the use of force by the use of law. we all know democracy starts to crumble if we break our common rules. in the european context we must respect the community method. the paradox of today’s debate is that strong rules and strong european institutions are sometimes seen as a threat to member states. in fact the opposite is true: the rule of law and common institutions protect member states, especially the smaller ones. second, we need to strike the right balance between solidarity and responsibility. the european union is a community based on solidarity. solidarity is part of its very essence. finland wants to play its own part. our share of the eu budget will increase, and we accept that as an element of european solidarity. finland is also shouldering its responsibility to assist countries in need of financial assistance. we do this through the crisis management instruments and direct loans. but solidarity must go hand in hand with the member state’s own responsibility. we all have to do our own homework. we all have to take difficult political decisions when they are due. europe should help when help is needed. but each member state has to bear the ultimate responsibility for keeping its own finances in order. those who decide about expenditure must collect the revenues. national governments and parliaments are ultimately responsible for national reforms. the third point is that to make europe stronger, we need deeper integration. my government will support deeper integration as long as it is fair to all member states and benefits the union and the whole of europe as an entity. our most pressing challenge is to create new jobs. too many europeans – especially young people – are without work today. unemployment is a problem for the whole of society, but first and foremost it hits those individuals who are struggling to make ends meet. last week i visited lisbon, where i had the opportunity to talk with university students. i was impressed by their enormous talent and energy. but the discussion revealed how worried they were about the future. i know how they feel. i remember finland’s own financial crisis all too well. in the early 1990s, almost 20% of finns were jobless. finland was on the brink of insolvency. over 10% of our gdp was shaved off in just a few years. at the time, i was a university student myself. i remember thinking we would never get a job or own a home. we did not want to graduate, because it was safer to stay in the university. when i now think back to those bleak years, even the images in my mind are black and white. finland managed to get through the crisis, but in many ways, we are still paying the social price for it. so, ladies and gentlemen let us make jobs our top european priority. we all know there is no shortcut to creating new jobs in a sustainable manner. if there was, surely we would have taken it already. i fully support the proposal to allocate eur six billion from the eu budget to fighting youth unemployment, and i am pleased the european council endorsed the youth guarantee concept. it is essential we keep all our young people on board. what matters the most is our ability to meet global competition. europe must become more competitive so that businesses continue to make new investments and create new jobs here. europe has to regain the upper hand in new technologies and industries. the key to europe’s economic future lies with reform and openness. we have to work with the markets, not against them. mr president, we have taken impressive steps to overhaul the eu’s economic governance. i would like to thank this house for the important role it has played in passing critical legislation, such as the six pack and the two pack. the implementation of the rules will require sometimes difficult and painful reforms nationally. structural reforms will not bear fruit overnight, but reforms are the most effective and most sustainable economic stimulus in the long run. if we all play by the new rules, our economies will get stronger. this is not just economic theory, it is plain common sense. arvoisa puhemies, sisämarkkinat ja sisäisen vapaakaupan edistäminen ovat euroopan integraation ruisleipä. tässä olemme päässeet pitkälle, mutta emme riittävän pitkälle. tavarat liikkuvat euroopassa hyvin, mutta palvelut eivät. siksi palveludirektiivin toimeenpanoa on välttämätöntä tehostaa. digitaaliset sisämarkkinat tarjoavat valtavan mahdollisuuden luoda uutta työtä ja kasvua. komissio arvioi, että eu:n talous kasvaisi tällä toimenpiteellä 500 miljardilla eurolla vuoteen 2020 mennessä. olisi siis sulaa hulluutta jättää potentiaali käyttämättä. sähköinen kauppa ja digitaaliset sisällöt tarvitsevat kiireesti toimivat sisämarkkinat. niiden rakentaminen on jo alkanut – osin euroopan parlamentin ansiosta – mutta työ etenee liian hitaasti. tarvitsemme uutta, älykästä sääntelyä, joka raivaa kaupan esteitä ja tukee digitaalisen talouden dynaamisuutta. monsieur le président, nous avons le devoir de libérer le potentiel énorme de notre commerce extérieur pour créer des emplois. la commission européenne a estimé que la réalisation d'un plan ambitieux de libre-échange créera deux millions d'emplois en europe. nous avons ouvert le marché et donné aux entreprises européennes les opportunités dont elles ont besoin. européerna har både den skicklighet och den kreativitet som krävs för att nå framgång på den globala marknaden. vi måste tro på oss själva. om vi tyr oss till protektionism och bygger hinder, isolerar vi oss bara från pulsen och händelserna inom världsekonomin. inledandet av frihandels- och investeringsförhandlingar med förenta staterna och japan är de bästa nyheterna på länge. låt oss hålla farten uppe och inte fastna i detaljer. it is essential that we strengthen economic and monetary union. our immediate priority is to finalise banking union. to me, banking union is a good example of fair integration. it is about curbing reckless risk-taking and protecting taxpayers from having to rescue oversized and under-capitalised banks. i have three final points on how to make europe fit for the future. first, we need a truly integrated european energy market. energy is the lifeblood of the economy. global competition for energy is getting fiercer. europe needs to get its act together and take the internal energy market seriously. we also need to move away from subsidies that distort the market. we need more investment in energy infrastructure. to drive investment in low-emission alternatives, we need to restore the effect of the emissions trading system, which you were deliberating yesterday evening. second, we need concrete steps in european security and defence policy. europe has to take more responsibility for its security, which means we must learn to work more closely together. we need closer cooperation to meet security challenges, to overcome the financial limits and to provide our security and defence industry with a wider home market to grow. i am looking forward to our december discussions in the european council. third, i would just say that we must keep enlargement on our agenda. the european union must remain open to deserving candidates. the next european elections will be held in a year’s time. this election is of exceptional importance. it will be a test of the democratic legitimacy of the european union. its outcome will show the future direction of our common european project. european integration has never been challenged as it is today. we have a lot to defend and we should do this with pride. european integration has proved that it can deliver peace, stability and well-being to european citizens on a scale never seen before in this continent. it will continue to do so. the european union will emerge from the crisis stronger. it will take some time and the road ahead will not be easy. we must focus on energy and what unites us, not on what separates us. we must build mutual trust, because together we are stronger than any of us would be alone. we must focus on reinforcing the fairness of european integration. fair integration is the best way to build a strong europe and to regain people’s trust in the european project. president of the commission. − mr president, mr prime minister, honourable members. before i begin, i should like to express, on behalf of the commission, our deep sympathy with the victims and with the families of those killed and injured in the violent attacks in boston yesterday. we condemn all forms of violence, and we stand in solidarity with our american friends on this sad day. it is a pleasure for me to say some words here today, when the prime minister of finland, mr katainen, is debating the future direction of the european union with the european parliament. i want to start by thanking the finnish prime minister for his very important, personal contribution to the european project. jyrki katainen has shown a strong commitment to strengthening democracy, transparency and dialogue in the european union. in short, the finnish prime minister and the country he represents stand for a european union which is, first and foremost, a community of values. this brings me to the first point which i wanted to make this morning, which is that finland embodies the most fundamental concept at the heart of our union – the rule of law and the principle of equal rights. no matter what their size, economic weight, history or culture, our union is a union of member states joined together by common values and shared interests. it is a union that shows equal respect for rights and hears the voice of each and every member state. in this environment, finland has demonstrated that it is not size alone which moves the european debate forward but the strength of your ideas and the commitment and determination to see these ideas through. on issues ranging from enlargement to the single market or the digital agenda, from the union’s international trade relations to justice and home affairs, finland is a leading light in moving and shaping european policy. let me make a specific point on the rule of law and fairness. the prime minister rightly places great importance on these issues. so does the commission, especially at a time when reform is placing a burden on our societies. this is why we are pushing forward with our proposals to combat tax evasion and tax avoidance, which cost europe around eur 1 trillion per year in lost tax revenues. in other words, europe is losing tax revenues every year which amount to one full multiannual financial framework. this is money that we can ill afford and which increases the burden on the average, honest taxpayer. it is time to turn good intentions into action. that is why i call on the member states to reach a swift agreement on the commission’s proposals on savings tax and for a strong mandate to negotiate agreements with switzerland and other neighbours, as well as for a rapid reaction mechanism to tackle vat fraud. in the coming weeks i will be urging the member states to jointly commit to common actions and an agreed timeline to implement the recommendations on tax havens and aggressive tax planning which the commission made last december. i thank finland for its support on this issue, including its welcome initiative to host a joint seminar with the commission at the end of this month. in a recent speech on competitiveness which i made in dublin, i underlined the position of finland as the leading member state in the world economic forum global competitive index, in which finland ranked third in the world. across europe, as we seek to exit the current crisis and bolster europe’s long-term competitiveness, it is important that we look at finland and take on board the lessons from the finnish experience. these are long, hard lessons. following its domestic banking crisis in the 1990s, finland undertook a series of deep, difficult structural reforms in order to reshape its economy, regain international competitiveness and retain the principal elements of its social market economy. this process is one which many other member states are now following and which finland has been supporting by showing solidarity with these countries. finland is also playing an active role in the shaping of the banking union. events in cyprus show just how important this work is and how it is even more urgent than ever. i am pleased that, following the intensive work in the trialogues, there is now a final agreement on the single supervisory mechanism. the commission will bring forward proposals for a single resolution mechanism in june. the most important lesson in all of this is that it should not be seen as a one-off exercise: it is a day-to-day exercise. remaining competitive requires constant work, as finland has recognised and is currently demonstrating through its ongoing efforts. finland is engaged in a dialogue with its european partners, setting out its ideas and discussing its concerns as an active, engaged and thoughtful member of our union. i would like to thank the prime minister for his role in shaping this approach and for his very close cooperation and friendship. i would like to thank finland for its commitment to our union. (applause)
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president of parliament, mr president of the commission, mr prime minister, i also agree with the statements made by my predecessors on the boston bombing and i believe that we in the epp group have the will and the strength to fight this terrorism. as you said, we do not yet know where it comes from, but it does not stop, wherever it comes from, it is not normal that in a society where freedom reigns, people who have done nothing wrong, who are involved in sports, are killed simply because they want to express themselves freely through sport. i think that is unacceptable and that we must fight this terrorism very firmly. mr president, i have listened to you very carefully and, as you will not be surprised to learn, i agree with you on many points. but i would like to share some observations with you and ask you some questions. first of all, the direction of europe. europe is much more than a project - you said it - of economic integration. europe is also, above all, about shared values. you're right to call him back. today, without europe, it would surely be even worse. i've said it many times. just take a look at iceland, which went bankrupt. i do not deny the difficulties experienced in greece, spain and ireland. but where would these countries be without europe? i think, like you, that we must fight extremism and that the best way to do this is to speak the truth, to be responsible but also to show solidarity. we must also move towards greater european integration - we must not be afraid to say so in a difficult time of crisis when everyone wants to turn in on themselves - starting also with social and fiscal harmonization. it's not a bad word. but not towards a standardization which would be more of a disadvantage than an advantage. harmonizing is also about sharing our strengths. the weekly working time, the weeks of leave, the retirement age, social expenditure, all have to be worked out on the same basis. the single market has brought about a lot of progress, but because of these persistent national disparities, there have been a lot of negative effects. i know what i am talking about, as a businessman, with simply, on the other side of the rhine, the distortion of competition that we can call one way or another. of 60 million turnover in my company, there would be 1.2 million difference in charges if my slaughterhouse was in kehl. i say it every day so we know it. so we need tax and social harmonization, otherwise it is not possible, and companies will be forced to move from where it is more expensive or they will close down. some of our citizens have lost their jobs, some businesses have disappeared. the problem, ladies and gentlemen, is that today it is the member states, each in its own corner, which are the only ones competent to deal with these problems. so we need more europe and - i agree with you, mr prime minister - a fair europe. there is unemployment in europe but there are also jobs. the problem is, they're not necessarily in the same place. why not consider european solutions to unemployment? today, this is not a european competence. why not use the big picture that europe offers? in the field of education, training, research, or cohesion policy, we have the levers to move the mobility of workers forward. if we do not have european research, mr josé manuel, there is no point in distributing aid country by country on a research programme which is not european. i think it takes courage to go in that direction too. in order to improve the balance between workers and the labour market and to combat youth unemployment, we have supported the youth guarantee and are pleased that your government has joined it. but there is more to it. mr president, the majority of this parliament, like you, is in favour of a strong europe with strong states and a strong economy. to do that, all our rules must be enforced. we need more transparency, budgets must be balanced and deficits must be reduced because we can no longer live beyond our means. we must also tell the truth about this. we will thus restore the confidence needed for investment, but will this be enough? in some countries - hardest hit by the crisis - interest rates are such that a businessman, even if he has the best project, cannot finance it. i was in greece where a businessman, who had a project, said to me, "president, should i invest with an interest rate between 10 and 12 percent? " i said, "no, you can't invest in an economic portfolio at this rate of interest". that means that in this country we cannot create jobs. that is the real problem we have to fight. i wonder why, mr prime minister, if we are to overcome unemployment and especially youth unemployment, we must find something. i know this is probably going to shock some of you, but is it not time to think about responsible mutualisation of part of the public debt in europe so that the interest rates for investors are the same across the countries? i'm not talking about standardization. so i ask you, mr. prime minister, if you have another remedy, we're taking it! it would be possible to reduce the cost of debt, to lower interest rates for entrepreneurs who create jobs and to channel some of our resources to investment. of course, such partial mutualisation must be accompanied by better governance, an awareness of the constraints of mutual guarantee to avoid disguised subsidies or the fact that some states have to pay for others. each state must ensure its solvency. this implies a real convergence of europe. we also need more coherence and therefore more integration. your speech, mr prime minister, is about the future of europe. i will end by saying a few words, but i am passionate about it because i am looking for jobs, mr president, and you know that i do not often exceed my speaking time. our history has proved it. the more we work together, the more integrated we are and the better our continent is doing and the more europe protects us!

in writing. the new challenges arising from the latest developments in the field of network and information security call for the extension of the competences of the european network and information security agency (enisa). in agreement with the european commission's proposal to extend the tasks of enisa, i voted in favour of this report which revises and extends the mandate of the agency. this proposal also updates its competence in the development of network and information security policies, its work as a facilitator of cooperation between member states, and its role in preventing and mitigating network and information security incidents between states. we, the members of the european parliament, were able to impose our views on the council on the question of the seat, with the establishment of an enisa 'antenna' in athens. we have also obtained an obligation on the board to create an executive board in order to increase efficiency and effectiveness.
in writing. i voted in favour of the chichester report which thoroughly revises the provisions governing enisa's powers. created in 2004, the agency is responsible for the network and information security of the european union. initially appointed for a period of four years, she was reappointed for a further seven years. in order to meet current challenges, in particular in terms of cybercrime, the powers of the agency have been strengthened. enisa will now be able to act on its own initiative.
in writing. the european network and information security agency (enisa) was established in 2004 to assist the commission and the member states in developing policies on network and information security. i voted in favour of the directive which aims to extend its powers to deal with new technologies which bring new challenges to network and information security. i also support the new international dimension of enisa, which will now be able to enter into direct contact with third countries and international organisations, for greater speed and efficiency.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of this report on the activities of the european agency for the safety of information networks (enisa). in line with the recommendations of the report, i believe it is important to give enisa new powers to meet the challenges arising from recent developments in the field of network and information security. the closer coordination of the agency with the national authorities and europol also seems to me to be an excellent thing. the report also calls for the enhancement of the effectiveness of enisa's governance, which is another priority that i fully support.
in writing. protecting networks and information means protecting our privacy and our everyday convenience. enisa is the agency responsible for protecting these networks. their importance in the provision of essential services, including energy, should be emphasised. but these networks face constantly evolving threats, both in form and in number. the report rightly emphasizes this: it is no longer time to think in terms of reaction, we must move to anticipation. i therefore welcome the fact that this text strengthens and extends the mandate of enisa. it had to be made more modern and, above all, more responsive to the new challenges it was facing.
in writing. cybercrime is a modern scourge, which is a sword of damocles for the industrial sector but also for the privacy of our citizens. in order to continue effectively the indispensable fight against cybercrime, it seems essential to strengthen the role of the european agency for network and information security and to extend its mandate. that is why i voted in favour of this report, which proposes to modernise and rationalise the agency.
in writing. on tuesday 16 april, i commented on the report by my colleague, mr giles chichester, on the european union agency for security and networks. i voted in favour of this report. the main issue was the headquarters of the agency, currently in heraklion, crete. arguing that the country's accessibility is poor and that social tensions are high, a number of countries and parliamentarians have been considering moving the agency's headquarters. although i am not a fan of this type of institution, i do not think it would be appropriate to change the seat in the present conditions in greece. it would have been a symbol of the abandonment of the greek people who were sent. my colleague's report calls for the siege in heraklion to be maintained, and for a technical centre in athens to be attached to it, which is, in the final analysis, rather positive.
in writing. i supported in plenary the report by my colleague giles chichester. the report was adopted by 626 votes in favour, 45 against and 16 abstentions. i'm glad you did. the report aimed to review in depth the tasks and competences of the european network and information security agency (enisa). enisa will now have new tasks. in particular, it will assist the european commission and the member states in the development of network and information security policies, and facilitate cooperation between member states - and between them and the european commission - to prevent network and information security incidents. finally, enisa will assist member states, european institutions and bodies in their efforts to collect, analyse and disseminate data on network and information security.
in writing. the new challenges in the field of network and information security made the adoption of this text necessary, and i voted in favour of it. the text will further assist the european commission and the member states in the development of their network and information security policies, in particular by strengthening the link with national data protection and privacy authorities, but also with europol.
in writing. i voted in favour of this proposal amending the proposal from the european parliament and the council establishing measures relating to the incidental catching of cetaceans in fisheries. it is necessary to clearly identify and control the powers conferred on the european commission in the field of fisheries. for this reason, they should be classified under the treaty on the functioning of the european union (tfeu) according to the new hierarchy of standards: either as measures which may be the subject of delegated acts (non-legislative acts of general application supplementing or amending certain non-essential elements of the legislative act) or as measures which may be the subject of implementing acts. both types of act are effective tools and can be adapted quickly to new situations. in this context, delegated acts should be aimed at the adaptation of the technical specifications and conditions of use of sound-absorbing devices, while implementing acts will be dedicated to the modalities of the procedure and the format of the reports that member states are required to establish.
in writing. the treaty of lisbon has conferred new delegated and implementing powers on the commission. i therefore voted in favour of this report, which aims to apply these new powers in practice to the accidental catching of cetaceans in fisheries. in this way the commission will be able to ensure the uniform application of the procedural conditions in each member state.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report by raül romeva i rueda, which seeks to amend the proposal for a council regulation laying down measures concerning the incidental catching of cetaceans. the purpose of the report is to identify the measures that fall under the scope of delegated acts and those that fall under the scope of implementing acts. i agree with the rapporteur who suggests the use of delegated acts to adapt the conditions and technical specifications for the use of sound suppression devices. i also fully support his desire to adopt stricter conditions for the use of delegated acts by the commission, as i am determined to defend the powers acquired by the european parliament in the fisheries field following the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon.
in writing. i voted in favour of this text, as it brings about a real simplification of the technocratic procedures in place so far. europe must not be here to add a new layer of constraints to the european fisheries sector, but on the contrary must lighten the bureaucratic burden on it in order to protect and strengthen this sector.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of this report which will allow for better protection of cetaceans. it makes it possible to adjust the legislation on the incidental capture of cetaceans by clarifying the european commission's powers in this area. the commission will thus be able to propose, by 2015, comprehensive legislation aimed at adapting to technical and scientific progress, for example, the noise deterrent devices described in annex 2. this adaptation is essential in view of the constant and worrying decline in the whale population.

in writing. this new economic agreement is, at first sight, not a bad agreement, since it is economically reasonable and encourages a sustainable management of available resources. however, local fishermen's unions have come forward on many occasions with a distasteful feeling that they were not included in the negotiations, a problem unfortunately recurring in the field of eu fisheries agreements with third countries. our future common fisheries policy has the potential to incorporate, for the first time, binding ecological criteria in the name of sustainable exploitation of fisheries resources. but this key paradigm shift must be made in close collaboration with the first parties concerned, and therefore the local fishermen, who are the guarantors of a successful ecological transition. the european parliament has now given its approval, and i encourage the competent authorities to work in good faith with their preferred partners, in a spirit of exchange, respect and adequate support for the healthy and endogenous development of local economies.
